text: PepsiCo, Inc. is a leading global beverage and convenient food company that was incorporated in Delaware in 1919 and reincorporated in North Carolina in 1986. The company operates through seven reportable segments: Frito-Lay North America (FLNA), Quaker Foods North America (QFNA), PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA), Latin America (LatAm), Europe, Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA), and Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China Region (APAC). FLNA produces and sells branded convenient foods such as Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, and Tostitos, sold to independent distributors and retailers, and operates a joint venture with Strauss Group to market Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads. QFNA produces and sells cereals, rice, pasta, and other branded foods like Cap’n Crunch, Life cereal, Quaker grits, and Quaker oatmeal, distributed through independent distributors and retailers. PBNA manufactures and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods under brands such as Aquafina, Diet Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Pepsi, and Propel, operating its own bottling and distribution facilities and also supplying to authorized and independent bottlers. PBNA also produces ready-to-drink tea and coffee through joint ventures with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks, and manufactures brands licensed from Keurig Dr Pepper and Dole Food Company, Inc. and Ocean Spray Cranberries, Inc. In the first quarter of 2022, PepsiCo sold its Tropicana, Naked, and other select juice brands to PAI Partners while retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in a new joint venture that operates across North America and Europe, with PepsiCo acting as the exclusive distributor for small-format and foodservice customers in the U.S. with chilled direct-store-delivery. LatAm markets and sells convenient food brands including Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, and Quaker products, and beverage brands such as 7UP, Gatorade, Pepsi, and San Carlos, sold to authorized and independent bottlers, distributors, and retailers, and also produces ready-to-drink tea via a joint venture with Unilever. Europe markets and sells convenient food brands like Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, and Quaker products, beverage brands including 7UP, Diet Pepsi, Pepsi Max, and Pepsi, and also produces SodaStream sparkling water makers and dairy products such as Agusha, Chudo, and Domik v Derevne, with ready-to-drink tea via a joint venture with Unilever. AMESA markets and sells convenient food brands such as Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, and Quaker products, and beverage brands including 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, and Pepsi, sold to authorized and independent bottlers and retailers, with ready-to-drink tea via a joint venture with Unilever. APAC markets and sells convenient food brands including BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, and Smith’s, and beverage brands such as 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, and Sting, sold to authorized and independent bottlers and retailers, and also produces ready-to-drink tea through a joint venture with Unilever. The company serves customers and consumers in more than 200 countries and territories. The aggregate market value of PepsiCo, Inc. Common Stock held by nonaffiliates as of June 11, 2021, was $203.9 billion, based on the closing sale price on that date. The number of shares of PepsiCo, Inc. Common Stock outstanding as of February 3, 2022, was 1,383,451,400.

Products are sold to authorized and independent bottlers, independent distributors, and retailers. In certain markets, AMESA operates its own bottling plants and distribution facilities. AMESA, either independently or in collaboration with third parties, produces, markets, distributes, and sells ready-to-drink tea products through an international joint venture with Unilever under the Lipton brand name. In the Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China Region, APAC produces, markets, distributes, and sells a range of convenient food brands including BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, and Smith’s, as well as Quaker-branded convenient foods, through consolidated businesses and noncontrolled affiliates. APAC also produces, markets, distributes, and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods under brands such as 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, and Sting, which are sold to authorized and independent bottlers, independent distributors, and retailers. APAC also produces, markets, distributes, and sells ready-to-drink tea products through the same international joint venture with Unilever under the Lipton brand name. Additionally, APAC licenses the Tropicana brand for co-branded juice products in China through a strategic alliance with Tingyi (Cayman Islands) Holding Corp. (Tingyi). Products are primarily distributed through direct-store-delivery (DSD), customer warehouse systems, distributor networks, and e-commerce platforms and mobile applications, with the method depending on customer needs, product characteristics, and local trade practices. DSD involves delivering beverages and convenient foods directly to retail stores, where they are merchandised by company employees or independent bottlers, enabling high visibility and appeal, especially for frequently restocked items responsive to in-store promotion. Some products are delivered to customer warehouses from company or third-party manufacturing and distribution centers, which is less costly and suitable for less fragile, non-perishable items with lower turnover. Many products are distributed via third-party distributors, which are effective for achieving broad reach by including multiple product lines on delivery vehicles, such as in the foodservice and vending business that delivers to restaurants, businesses, schools, and stadiums. Products are also available directly to consumers on company-owned and third-party e-commerce websites and mobile commerce apps. Key ingredients include apple, orange, and pineapple juice and concentrates, aspartame, corn, corn sweeteners, flavorings, flour, grapefruit, other fruits, oats, potatoes, raw milk, rice, seasonings, sucralose, sugar, vegetable and essential oils, and wheat, with water used in manufacturing. Packaging materials include plastic resins such as polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polypropylene, aluminum, glass, closures, cardboard, and paperboard cartons. The company integrates recyclability into product development and supports increased use of recycled content, including recycled PET. Fuel, electricity, and natural gas are essential commodities due to their use in operations and transportation. Specialists secure supplies, and no significant continuous shortages have been experienced; many inputs are purchased in the open market, with prices subject to fluctuation managed through fixed-price contracts, purchase orders, pricing agreements, and derivative instruments like swaps and futures. Supply risks are mitigated by sourcing from multiple geographies and suppliers. Price increases may or may not be passed on to customers. Investments are made to improve the sustainability of agricultural supply chains, including expanding sustainable farming practices globally. In 2021, higher-than-anticipated input costs and limited shortages occurred due to global inflation, supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, increased demand, and pandemic-related regulatory and macroeconomic factors, continuing into fiscal 2022. The company maintains voluntary supply chain finance agreements with global financial institutions, allowing suppliers to sell their receivables to these institutions, which had no material impact on business or financial results. The company owns numerous trademarks essential to its global operations, including Agusha, Amp Energy, Aquafina, Arto Lifewtr, BaiCaoWei, Bare, Bokomo, Bolt24, bubly, Cap’n Crunch, Ceres, Cheetos, Chester’s, Chipita, Chipsy, Chokis, Chudo, Cracker Jack, Crunchy, Diet Mountain Dew, Diet Mug, Diet Pepsi, Diet 7UP (outside the U.S.), Domik v Derevne, Doritos, Driftwell, Duyvis, Elma Chips, Emperador, Evolve, Frito-Lay, Fritos, Fruktovy Sad, G2, Gamesa, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Gatorlyte, Grandma’s, H2oh!, Health Warrior, Imunele, J7, Kas, Kurkure, Lay’s, Life, Lifewtr, Liquifruit, Lubimy, Mabel, Manzanita Sol, Marias Gamesa, Matutano, Mirinda, Miss Vickie’s, Moirs, Mother’s, Mountain Dew, Mountain Dew Code Red, Mountain Dew Game Fuel, Mountain Dew Kickstart, Mountain Dew Zero Sugar, MTN Dew Energy, Mug, Munchies, Muscle Milk, Near East, Off the Eaten Path, Paso de los Toros, Pasta Roni, Pearl Milling Company, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, Pepsi Max, Pepsi Zero Sugar, PopCorners, Pronutro, Propel, Quaker, Quaker Chewy, Quaker Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni, Rockstar Energy, Rold Gold, Ruffles, Sabritas, Safari, Sakata, Saladitas, San Carlos, Sandora, Santitas, Sasko, 7UP (outside the U.S.), 7UP Free (outside the U.S.), Sierra Mist, Sierra Mist Zero Sugar, Simba, Smartfood, Smith’s, Snack a Jacks, SoBe, SodaStream, Sonric’s, Spekko, Stacy’s, Sting, Stubborn Soda, SunChips, Toddy, Toddynho, Tostitos, V Water, Vesely Molochnik, Walkers, Weetbix, White Star, Ya, and Yachak. The company holds long-term licenses to use certain trademarks in specific markets, including Ocean Spray. It distributes Bang Energy drinks and various Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. brands, including Dr Pepper, Crush, and Schweppes in certain markets. Joint ventures in which the company has an ownership interest own or have rights to use trademarks such as Lipton, Sabra, and Starbucks. In the first quarter of 2022, the company sold its Tropicana, Naked, and other select juice brands to PAI Partners while retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in a newly formed joint venture operating across North America and Europe. In the U.S., PepsiCo acts as the exclusive distributor for the joint venture’s portfolio for small-format and foodservice customers with chilled direct-store-delivery. In 2022, the company will begin distributing Hard MTN Dew, an alcoholic beverage manufactured and owned by the Boston Beer Company, and has licensed the Hard MTN Dew trademark to Boston Beer Company, which has appointed the company as its distributor. Trademarks remain valid as long as they are used properly for identification, and the company emphasizes correct use. The company authorizes the use of its trademarks in joint ventures, bottling appointments, and retail merchandise to enhance brand awareness. The company owns or has licenses to use patents related to products, packaging, production processes, and equipment design and operation, some of which are licensed to others. Sales are seasonally affected, with peak performance in the third quarter due to holiday patterns and lowest activity in the first quarter, though seasonality has not materially impacted consolidated financial results. Customers include wholesale and other distributors, foodservice providers, grocery stores, drug stores, convenience stores, discount/dollar stores, mass merchandisers, membership stores, hard discounters, e-commerce retailers, and authorized independent bottlers. Independent bottlers typically receive exclusive contracts to sell and manufacture certain beverage products in specific geographic areas, granting the company the right to charge royalties for concentrate, finished goods, and Aquafina, and specifying required manufacturing processes to ensure quality. Distribution rights are also granted to independent bottlers for certain beverage products in defined geographic areas. The company provides financial incentives to customers, including volume-based rebates, product placement fees, promotions, and displays for independent distributors and retailers. For independent bottlers, incentives—referred to as bottler funding—are negotiated annually and support consumer incentives, advertising, new product launches, and vending and cooler equipment placement. Consumer incentives include pricing discounts and promotions, advertising support includes media programs for bottler marketing, new product support includes targeted consumer and retailer incentives and point-of-purchase materials, and vending and cooler equipment programs support the acquisition and placement of vending machines. The nature and type of programs vary annually. Changes in the retail landscape, including retail consolidation, growth in e-commerce and subscription services, integration of physical and digital operations, international expansion of hard discounters, and the economic environment—including the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic—have increased the importance of major customers. In 2021, sales to Walmart Inc. (Walmart) and its affiliates, including Sam’s Club (Sam’s), represented approximately 13% of consolidated net revenue across all divisions, including concentrate sales to bottlers used in finished goods sold to Walmart. Losing this customer would have a material adverse effect on the FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA divisions. The company competes in highly competitive beverage and convenient food markets against international companies operating in multiple regions, regional and local manufacturers, private label brands, and smaller companies selling micro-brands directly via e-commerce or locally-focused retailers. In the United States, The Coca-Cola Company is the primary beverage competitor. Other competitors include Campbell Soup Company, Conagra Brands, Inc., Hormel Foods Corporation, Kellogg Company, Keurig Dr Pepper Inc., The Kraft Heinz Company, Link Snacks, Inc., Mondelēz International, Inc., Monster Beverage Corporation, Nestlé S.A., Red Bull GmbH, and Utz Brands, Inc. Many convenient food products hold significant market leadership in the U.S. and globally. In 2021, the company and The Coca-Cola Company represented approximately 22% and 19%, respectively, of the U.S. liquid refreshment beverage category by estimated retail sales in measured channels, according to Information Resources, Inc. However, The Coca-Cola Company has a significant carbonated soft drink share advantage in many markets outside the U.S. Competition is based on brand recognition, loyalty, taste, price, value, quality, product variety, innovation, distribution, advertising, marketing, packaging, convenience, service, and the ability to anticipate and respond to consumer preferences, including health and wellness and sustainability, as well as e-commerce trends. Success depends on effective promotion, new product development and reformulations, production efficiency, technology integration, advertising, marketing, packaging, pricing, vending equipment, and brand development. The company believes its brand strength, innovation, marketing, product quality, and flexible distribution network enable effective competition. The company conducts global research and development to meet customer and consumer needs and accelerate growth, focusing on creating preferred products through new technologies, ingredients, flavors, and substrates; improving manufacturing processes to reduce costs and environmental impact; reducing added sugars, sodium, or saturated fat; offering products with functional ingredients like whole grains, fruits, vegetables, dairy, protein, fiber, micronutrients, and hydration; developing sustainable packaging, including recyclable, compostable, biodegradable, or otherwise sustainable options and reducing plastic use; improving marketing, merchandising, and dispensing equipment; expanding beyond the bottle portfolio, including for SodaStream; investing in technology and digitalization such as artificial intelligence and data analytics for consumer insights; strengthening omnichannel capabilities, especially in e-commerce; and reducing environmental impact through reduced water use and climate impact across the value chain. Research centers are located globally in Brazil, China, India, Ireland, Mexico, Russia, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States, leveraging consumer insights, food science, and engineering to innovate the beverage and convenient food portfolio. The company’s operations are subject to various federal, state, and local laws in the U.S. and in over 200 other countries and territories, including the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, Food Safety Modernization Act, Occupational Safety and Health Act, environmental protection laws, Federal Motor Carrier Safety Act, Federal Trade Commission Act, Lanham Act, competition and trade practices laws, employment laws such as the Equal Employment Opportunity Act and Fair Labor Standards Act, alcohol sale and distribution laws, data privacy laws including the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 and California Privacy Rights Act, customs and foreign trade laws, school product regulations, supply chain laws such as the 2010 California Transparency in Supply Chains Act, tax laws, and the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and Trade Sanctions Reform and Export Enhancement Act. The company also complies with state and local statutes, including Proposition 65 in California, which requires a warning on products containing substances known to cause cancer or birth defects unless below a safe harbor level.

PepsiCo is subject to a wide range of federal, state, and international laws and regulations that govern various aspects of its operations. These include the Equal Employment Opportunity Act, the National Labor Relations Act, and the Fair Labor Standards Act, which relate to employment and overtime compensation; laws concerning the sale and distribution of alcohol beverages; data privacy and personal data protection regulations, such as the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 and the California Privacy Rights Act; customs and foreign trade laws, including import/export regulations and tariffs; laws restricting the sale of certain products in schools; supply chain regulations, such as the 2010 California Transparency in Supply Chains Act; and laws related to tax payments. The company must also comply with the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and the Trade Sanctions Reform and Export Enhancement Act. Additionally, PepsiCo is subject to state and local statutes, including Proposition 65 in California, which requires warnings on products containing substances known to cause cancer or birth defects if above a safe harbor level. Outside the United States, the company faces numerous laws related to food safety, international trade, supply chain, occupational health and safety, competition, anti-corruption (including the U.K. Bribery Act), and data privacy (such as the European Union General Data Protection Regulation). Compliance with competition and anti-corruption laws is particularly important due to PepsiCo’s competitive position in many jurisdictions. The company relies on legal and operational compliance programs, in-house and external legal counsel, and other experts to ensure adherence to global laws. Certain jurisdictions have imposed or are considering imposing new or increased taxes on the manufacture, distribution, or sale of PepsiCo’s products, ingredients, or substances, with tax structures varying—some applying to all beverages, including non-caloric ones, while others target beverages with caloric sweeteners, using single, graduated, or flat tax rates based on sugar content. Some jurisdictions have also introduced or are considering product labeling, warning, or marketing restrictions, such as highlighting health concerns, warning against certain ingredients, restricting sales to specific age groups, or limiting product availability. Similar or more restrictive measures may be proposed in the future. PepsiCo is also subject to environmental laws in the U.S. and abroad, including the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act, and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, as well as similar regulations outside the U.S. Concerns over environmental, social, and governance issues, including climate change, are leading to new or stricter requirements to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, limit commercial water use, and mandate reporting of environmental metrics. PepsiCo adheres to all applicable environmental laws, maintains global environmental compliance programs, and makes necessary expenditures for compliance and sustainability goals. While these costs have not materially impacted its business, financial condition, or operations, future changes in environmental regulations or compliance costs could adversely affect financial performance. The company also faces environmental remediation and indemnification obligations from historical activities or acquired businesses, which, though not currently material, cannot be predicted with certainty. PepsiCo employs approximately 309,000 people worldwide as of December 25, 2021, including about 129,000 in the United States, and is party to numerous collective bargaining agreements, with generally good employee relations. Protecting employee safety, health, and well-being is a top priority, with investments in technologies like fleet telematics, distracted driving prevention, and wearable ergonomic devices to reduce workplace injuries. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the company maintained health and safety protocols, provided personal protective equipment, and enabled testing, especially for frontline workers. PepsiCo believes its culture of diversity, equity, and inclusion is a competitive advantage, enhancing innovation, talent attraction, and reputation. As of December 25, 2021, 27% of the global workforce was female, with 43% of management roles held by women; 45% of the U.S. workforce was racially/ethnically diverse, and 31% of U.S. managerial roles were held by racially/ethnically diverse individuals. Seven of the CEO’s direct reports are racially/ethnically diverse or female. The company supports associate development through global training and development programs, including career plans, mentoring, and in-house learning such as PEP U Degreed, with over 1,000,000 training hours completed in 2021. PepsiCo files annual, quarterly, and current reports, proxy statements, and other disclosures with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and these filings are available on the SEC’s website at http://www.sec.gov. The company also makes its reports available free of charge on its corporate website at http://www.pepsico.com as soon as reasonably practicable after filing. Investors are encouraged to review information posted on these platforms, which may be deemed material, and the company may update its communication channels, with such changes posted on its website. Information on the website is not incorporated into or part of any SEC filing. The document also includes a section on risk factors, noting that ongoing uncertainty from the COVID-19 pandemic continues to affect business operations, including changes in consumer demand, shifts in channel preferences (such as increased e-commerce), supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, and rising operational costs due to remote work, PPE, sanitation, and inflation. The pandemic has also increased vulnerability to cyberattacks and disrupted information technology infrastructure. Economic uncertainty has affected access to capital and credit markets. Reduced demand for products due to shifts in consumer preferences—such as changes in demographics, pricing, product quality, packaging concerns, or nutrition-related perceptions—can lead to reduced sales, inventory write-offs, or eroded competitiveness. Damage to the company’s reputation, due to ethical, environmental, social, or governance failures, product safety issues, advertising controversies, or social media responses, can decrease demand and harm business performance. Product recalls, due to mislabeling, spoilage, allergens, adulteration, or contamination, can result in financial losses, inventory destruction, lost sales, and reduced consumer confidence, while failures in quality oversight may lead to litigation, investigations, fines, or criminal liability. Consumer loss of confidence in product quality or safety can also negatively impact the business.

Product recalls due to quality or safety issues—such as mislabeling, misbranding, spoilage, undeclared allergens, adulteration, or contamination—can negatively impact the business by causing financial losses, destroying inventory, and leading to lost sales during periods of product unavailability. Such issues, whether stemming from non-compliance with food safety laws or other causes, may also erode consumer confidence, reduce demand, disrupt production and delivery, increase costs including fines or judgments, and harm the company’s reputation, especially as it expands into new categories like nuts and meat convenient foods globally and the distribution of alcoholic beverages in the United States. Failure to maintain proper oversight of product quality or safety can lead to recalls, litigation, government investigations, or civil or criminal proceedings, resulting in fines, penalties, damages, or liability. Even if unrelated to specific products, a general loss of consumer confidence in product quality, safety, or integrity can adversely affect the business. The company competes with international beverage and convenient food firms, regional and local manufacturers, private label brands, and small businesses selling micro brands via e-commerce or local retailers. In many markets, including the United States, The Coca-Cola Company is the primary beverage competitor. Competition is based on brand recognition, loyalty, taste, price, value, quality, product variety, innovation, distribution, advertising, marketing, packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to consumer trends. Business performance can be harmed if the company fails to promote or develop existing products, introduce and market new ones effectively, adopt new technologies like artificial intelligence and data analytics, strengthen digital marketing capabilities, or respond to supply disruptions, pricing pressure, or competitive actions. Failure to attract, develop, and retain a highly skilled and diverse workforce—particularly in areas like e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics—can deplete institutional knowledge, erode competitive advantages, increase employee costs, and damage reputation, especially if underrepresented communities are not adequately supported. Water scarcity, due to limited availability, climate change, or increasing regulatory and consumer pressure, can disrupt supply chains, affect operations, raise compliance and production costs, lead to facility interruptions or relocations, hinder water use goals, damage the company’s environmental image, or harm its reputation. Changes in the retail landscape—such as growth in e-commerce and hard discounters—can negatively affect the business if the company fails to maintain strong relationships with these channels or traditional retailers, especially as key customers increase their e-commerce sales. Expanding direct-to-consumer e-commerce capabilities profitably is also a challenge. Retail consolidation in North America, Europe, and Latin America, where large buyers have increased purchasing power, can reduce the company’s competitiveness and weaken smaller customers’ ability to purchase products, leading to lost orders or reduced payments. Maintaining strong relationships with key customers, such as Walmart, is essential; disputes, changes in their financial condition, significant sales declines, or customer loss can harm the business. Disruptions in manufacturing or supply chains—due to civil unrest, political instability, limited supplier availability, or seasonal shortages—can increase costs and interrupt product supply. Raw materials, including agricultural commodities, fuel, packaging (like recycled PET), transportation, labor, and other inputs are subject to price volatility and supply fluctuations from factors such as demand changes, inflation, weather, disease (e.g., greening disease in citrus), labor shortages (e.g., truck drivers), strikes, tariffs, trade barriers, port congestion, cybersecurity incidents, political uncertainty, terrorism, or currency fluctuations. Many raw materials are purchased in the open market, and unexpected or significant price increases may prevent the company from raising product prices or hedging effectively, leading to reduced revenue, margins, and operating results. Political and social conditions—such as election outcomes, government shutdowns, hostilities, or protests—can create uncertainty in regulations, tariffs, environmental policies, tax laws, and currency exchange rates, affecting demand and operations. In certain U.S. and global cities, prolonged protests or demonstrations, especially related to elections or civil rights, may disrupt operations, including distribution and raw material supply, due to government actions. Growth in developing and emerging markets—such as Mexico, Russia, the Middle East, China, South Africa, Brazil, and India—depends on product acceptance, cultural fit, distribution methods, and market conditions, but these markets face risks including economic instability, political unrest, war, terrorism, sanctions, foreign ownership restrictions, nationalization, government-mandated closures, import/export restrictions, currency devaluation or demonetization, complex compliance with laws like the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act or the U.K. Bribery Act, and weak legal systems. Failure to expand successfully or manage these risks can reduce returns on capital. Unfavorable economic conditions—such as recessions, inflation, volatile commodity markets, labor shortages, credit contraction, or currency fluctuations—can impact interest rates, taxes, pension costs, and overall financial stability, affecting both the company and its business partners. Future cyber incidents—such as cyberattacks, ransomware, denial-of-service attacks, social engineering, or supply chain compromises through software updates or compromised supplier accounts—can disrupt operations, compromise data, lead to financial losses, litigation, regulatory investigations, fines, reputational damage, or employee morale issues. These risks extend to third-party providers, including suppliers and cloud service providers, whose systems or failures can indirectly impact the company. Although past incidents have not materially affected operations, future events could have significant consequences. Despite investments in network security, disaster recovery, and employee training, there is no guarantee that systems will be fully protected. Insurance may cover some costs but may not cover all losses or reputational damage. Strategic transactions—such as acquisitions, joint ventures, divestitures, or distribution agreements—carry risks including failure to achieve expected synergies, delays in approvals, difficulties in integrating operations or IT systems, challenges in retaining key personnel, maintaining compliance with internal controls and anti-bribery laws, managing tax costs, preserving customer relationships, or handling differing interests among joint venture partners.

The success of strategic transactions, including the recent completion of the Juice Transaction, depends on our ability to realize expected returns, benefits, cost savings, or synergies within the anticipated time frame or at all, as well as receiving necessary consents, clearances, and approvals. Risks associated with such transactions include difficulties in integrating manufacturing, distribution, sales, accounting, financial reporting, and administrative support activities and information technology systems with our company, or in separating such personnel, activities, and systems during divestitures; operating under new business models or in new categories or territories; motivating, recruiting, and retaining executives and key employees; conforming controls (including internal control over financial reporting and disclosure controls and procedures) and policies (including environmental, health and safety, and anti-bribery compliance); retaining existing customers and attracting new ones; managing tax costs or inefficiencies; maintaining good relations with divested or refranchised businesses in our supply or sales chain; offsetting revenue losses from divested brands or businesses; managing the impact of decisions or actions by joint venture partners with differing interests; and other unanticipated problems or liabilities, such as contingent liabilities and litigation. Failure to successfully complete or manage these transactions or to effectively manage associated risks can have adverse effects on our business. Our reliance on third-party service providers—such as cloud data providers for payroll processing, health and benefit administration, and finance and accounting functions—can negatively impact our business. If these providers fail to meet their contractual, regulatory, or other obligations or if we inadequately monitor their performance, we may fail to achieve expected cost savings or efficiencies, incur additional costs to correct errors, experience business disruption, systems performance degradation, processing inefficiencies, security breaches leading to loss or damage of intellectual property or sensitive data, incorrect or adverse financial reporting, litigation, claims, regulatory proceedings, fines, penalties, remediation costs, reputational damage, or negative employee morale—all of which can harm our business. We are also advancing a multi-year phased business transformation to migrate financial processing systems to enterprise-wide solutions, which has led to and could continue to result in systems outages and operating inefficiencies. If we fail to allocate and manage sufficient resources to build and sustain the necessary information technology infrastructure or fail to achieve expected benefits from this initiative, our business could be adversely affected. Climate change poses risks to our business and reputation, as it may reduce agricultural productivity and availability or increase pricing for key commodities like potatoes, sugar cane, corn, wheat, rice, oats, oranges, and fruit-derived oils; it may also increase the frequency or severity of natural disasters and extreme weather, impairing production, disrupting supply chains, or affecting product demand. Additionally, many jurisdictions are implementing environmental policies related to climate change, greenhouse gas emissions, energy use, and sustainability—including single-use plastics—leading to new or increased legal and regulatory requirements, such as carbon pricing, which could significantly raise costs and require additional investments in facilities and equipment. Failure to meet environmental goals or perceived inaction on climate change can lead to adverse publicity, reducing product demand and damaging our reputation. Strikes or work stoppages, due to collective bargaining agreements, can impair manufacturing and distribution, lead to lost sales, increased costs, and hinder operational changes or strategic adaptation, all of which can negatively affect our business. Financial risks include failure to realize benefits from productivity initiatives, such as shared service models, which may result in business disruptions, employee distraction, reduced morale, unexpected attrition, difficulty attracting or retaining key personnel, and negative publicity—leading to adverse financial performance if expected savings are not achieved. A deterioration in assumptions about future business performance, such as competitive or macroeconomic conditions or changes in the weighted-average cost of capital, can trigger impairment charges that harm results of operations. Exchange rate fluctuations, due to inflation, monetary policies, currency controls, or restrictions, impact financial performance because our consolidated financial statements are in U.S. dollars, and we pay for raw materials and ingredients in multiple currencies. A downgrade or potential downgrade of our credit ratings—based on factors like cash generation, indebtedness, shareholder distributions, and broader economic or industry conditions—can increase borrowing costs, impair access to capital and credit markets, reduce liquidity, and limit access to commercial paper, forcing reliance on more expensive debt financing, all of which can harm financial performance. Legal, tax, and regulatory risks include taxes on products, particularly beverages, imposed or considered in jurisdictions like Canada, where a flat tax of 0.20 Canadian dollars (0.16 U.S. dollars) per liter on sugar-sweetened beverages was enacted on September 1, 2022, which can increase product costs, reduce consumption, and lead to negative publicity. Limitations on marketing or sale, such as warning labels in Argentina and Colombia requiring disclosure of high sugar, sodium, or saturated fat content, or color-coded labeling, can reduce consumption, cause negative publicity, or lead consumers to believe our products do not meet health needs. Laws and regulations on plastics or packaging, including extended producer responsibility, plastic taxes, bans on single-use plastics, bottle cap tethering, and minimum recycled content requirements (e.g., in the European Union, Peru, and U.S. states), can increase product costs, affect demand, result in negative publicity, and require investments in alternative or less plastic packaging. Failure to comply with personal data protection laws—such as the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation and California’s California Consumer Privacy Act—can lead to litigation, fines, penalties, and reputational damage due to inconsistent or evolving regulations. Increases in income tax rates, changes in tax laws, or disagreements with tax authorities—especially amid global proposals for a 15% minimum tax rate and profit reallocation—can increase tax uncertainty, compliance costs, and adverse financial impacts, particularly as tax audits and disputes may result in outcomes different from historical provisions. If we fail to protect our intellectual property—such as ingredient formulas, trademarks, patents, or trade secrets—our competitive position and product value could be reduced, and we may face litigation, damages, injunctions, inventory write-offs, or restrictions on product development or sales due to past or future infringement claims. Our business is subject to numerous laws and regulations covering production, storage, distribution, labeling, advertising, quality, safety, packaging, environmental, social, and governance matters, including climate change, and compliance with competition and anti-corruption laws. New laws, regulatory changes, or differing standards across markets can increase compliance and production costs. For example, growing societal attention to environmental, social, and governance issues has led to new regulations, and entering new markets—such as the U.S. alcoholic beverage distribution or global nuts and meat convenient foods—exposes us to additional regulatory burdens. If one jurisdiction imposes new regulations affecting our products, others may follow. Non-compliance can result in criminal or civil actions, including fines, injunctions, product recalls, penalties, disgorgement, or activity restrictions. Additionally, third-party studies—regardless of scientific validity—on the health effects of ingredients or packaging have led to or could lead to new taxes, regulations, or lawsuits that adversely affect our business. Potential liabilities and costs from litigation remain a significant risk.

Increasing governmental and societal attention to environmental, social, and governance issues has led to and may continue to lead to new laws or regulatory requirements. The entry into new markets or product categories, such as the planned entry into the alcoholic beverage industry as a distributor in the United States and expansion into the nuts and meat convenient foods categories globally, has resulted in and could continue to result in additional regulations, increasing compliance costs. If one jurisdiction introduces or proposes new laws or regulations affecting the manufacture, distribution, or sale of the company’s products, other jurisdictions may follow. Failure to comply with such laws or regulations can result in criminal or civil enforcement actions, including fines, injunctions, product recalls, penalties, disgorgement of profits, or activity restrictions, all of which could negatively impact the business. Additionally, third-party studies—regardless of their scientific validity—claiming health implications related to certain ingredients or substances in products or packaging have resulted in and could continue to result in new taxes, regulations, or lawsuits that could adversely affect the business. The company and its subsidiaries are involved in various litigation, claims, legal or regulatory proceedings, inquiries, and investigations, including matters related to advertising, marketing, product labels, ingredients, personal injury, property damage, intellectual property, privacy, employment, tax, insurance, environmental, social, and governance issues, and compliance with applicable laws. These matters are inherently uncertain, and there is no assurance that the company will successfully defend itself or that its assessment of the materiality, likely outcomes, or potential losses will match the final results. Responding to these matters—even if ultimately non-meritorious—requires significant expense and resource allocation and may lead to adverse publicity that harms the company’s reputation or brand image. Any of these factors could adversely affect the business. PepsiCo faces various risks related to commodities, climate change, international operations, taxes and regulations, and market conditions, all of which are influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic and shifts in consumer behavior. Many of the commodities used in production and transportation are purchased in the open market, and their prices fluctuate due to factors such as the pandemic, adverse weather, supply chain disruptions, and labor shortages. To manage commodity price risk, PepsiCo uses fixed-price contracts, purchase orders, pricing agreements, and derivative instruments like swaps and futures. In 2021, transportation and commodity costs exceeded expectations and are expected to continue in 2022. The company manages exposure to commodity prices through hedging and other strategies, with commodity derivatives having a total notional value of $1.6 billion as of December 25, 2021, and $1.1 billion as of December 26, 2020. A 10% decrease in underlying commodity prices would have reduced net unrealized gains by $177 million in 2021, which would be offset by lower commodity purchase costs. In terms of climate change, certain jurisdictions have imposed or are considering new or increased regulations on greenhouse gas emissions and carbon pricing, which could lead to higher compliance costs and investments in facilities and equipment, though the scope, nature, and timing of such regulations remain unpredictable. International operations are exposed to economic, political, and social instability, civil unrest, natural disasters, currency fluctuations, and debt issues, particularly in developing and emerging markets such as Argentina, Brazil, China, Mexico, the Middle East, Russia, and Turkey. Taxes and regulations on products or packaging vary by jurisdiction and may apply to all beverages or only those with caloric sweeteners, and some target packaging types or promote sustainability, recycling, or waste reduction. These regulations, including labeling requirements introduced in Mexico, vary in scope and form, and their impact on financial results is difficult to predict. The retail landscape has shifted due to the growth of e-commerce, mobile commerce, subscription services, and the expansion of hard discounters, with consumers increasingly turning to online purchasing, especially due to the pandemic. PepsiCo monitors these changes and works to strengthen its global e-commerce and digital capabilities. The company employs an integrated risk management framework overseen by the Board of Directors, which includes specific committees for audit, compensation, governance, and sustainability. The PepsiCo Risk Committee (PRC), composed of senior management, identifies, assesses, and addresses key risks, while division and country-specific committees manage business-specific risks. The Risk Management Office provides analytical support and communication across all levels. Market risks include commodity prices, foreign exchange rates, and interest rates, which are managed through productivity initiatives, global purchasing programs, and hedging. Foreign exchange risks are significant, with operations outside the U.S. generating 44% of consolidated net revenue in 2021, and Mexico, Russia, Canada, China, the U.K., and South Africa accounting for about 23% of that revenue. Favorable foreign exchange contributed 1 percentage point to net revenue growth in 2021 due to appreciation in the Mexican peso, Canadian dollar, and South African rand. An unfavorable 10% change in exchange rates would have reduced net unrealized gains by $278 million, offset by an inverse change in underlying exposure. The total notional value of foreign currency derivatives was $2.8 billion as of December 25, 2021, and $1.9 billion as of December 26, 2020. Net investment hedges had a total notional value of $2.1 billion as of December 25, 2021 and $2.7 billion as of December 26, 2020. Interest rate derivatives had a total notional value of $2.1 billion as of December 25, 2021 and $3.0 billion as of December 26, 2020. A 1-percentage-point increase in interest rates would have decreased net interest expense by $47 million in 2021 due to higher cash and short-term investment levels. Inflation, deflation, and recessionary conditions affect product demand and pricing. The company uses non-GAAP financial measures internally to support operating and strategic decisions, including the preparation of the annual operating plan, evaluation of business performance, and compensation determinations for certain employees. The company evaluates performance on operating profit and net income attributable to PepsiCo per common share – diluted, adjusted for items affecting comparability, on a constant currency basis, which assumes constant foreign exchange rates from the prior-year period. Return on invested capital (ROIC) is calculated as net income attributable to PepsiCo plus after-tax interest expense, divided by the sum of quarterly average debt obligations and quarterly average common shareholders’ equity. Net ROIC, excluding items affecting comparability, adjusts ROIC for quarterly average cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, after-tax interest income, and items affecting comparability. The company’s critical accounting policies and estimates include revenue recognition, goodwill and other intangible assets, income tax expense and accruals, and pension and retiree medical plans. Revenue is recognized when performance obligations are satisfied, typically upon shipment or delivery, with control transferred based on written sales terms without return rights. For DSD and certain warehouse-distributed products, damaged or out-of-date products are replaced, and reserves are recorded based on estimates. Products are sold for cash or on credit, with payment terms typically within 30 days in the U.S. and 30 to 90 days internationally, with early payment discounts. Credit loss exposure is estimated based on past due accounts, write-off history, aging of receivables, customer data analysis, and forward-looking information, including the impact of global economic uncertainty related to the pandemic. Sales incentives and discounts, including those for in-store displays, shelf space, and promotions, are primarily accounted for as revenue reductions. Accruals are established during the year for annual target-based incentives, based on contract terms and historical experience, requiring management judgment on customer and consumer performance. Differences between estimated and actual incentive costs are generally insignificant and recognized in the period determined. Advertising and marketing costs based on annual targets are recognized as incurred. Goodwill and intangible assets are determined in business combinations by assigning consideration to identifiable assets and liabilities, with any excess recorded as goodwill. Fair value determination requires significant estimates and assumptions, including those related to the pandemic, based on factors such as marketplace participants, product life cycles, market share, consumer awareness, brand history, future cash flows, and discount rates. A brand is considered to have an indefinite life if it has a history of strong revenue and cash flow performance and the company has the intent and ability to maintain that performance.

Actual incentive costs are typically negligible and are recognized in earnings during the period they are determined. Brand development costs are expensed as incurred, and brands or other intangible assets acquired in business combinations are assigned fair values based on estimated future cash flows, with any excess recorded as goodwill. Determining fair value involves significant estimates and assumptions, including those related to the COVID-19 pandemic, such as marketplace participants, product life cycles, market share, consumer awareness, brand history, future expansion, and discount rates. A brand is considered to have an indefinite life if it has a strong history of revenue and cash flow and if the company intends and is able to support it with marketplace spending for the foreseeable future; otherwise, brands are amortized over expected useful lives ranging from 20 to 40 years, based on factors like market share, consumer awareness, brand history, regulatory restrictions, and macroeconomic conditions. Franchise rights acquired in prior acquisitions, which provide exclusive and perpetual rights to manufacture and distribute beverages in specified territories, are evaluated for useful life; due to existing perpetual bottling arrangements and the absence of legal, regulatory, contractual, competitive, or economic factors limiting their duration, certain rights are considered indefinite-lived. Franchise rights not deemed indefinite-lived are amortized over the remaining contractual period. Indefinite-lived intangible assets and goodwill are not amortized and are assessed for impairment at least annually during the third quarter, or more frequently if indicators suggest the carrying value may not be recoverable. A qualitative assessment first determines if it is more likely than not that impairment exists, considering macroeconomic conditions (including those related to the COVID-19 pandemic), industry and competitive conditions, legal and regulatory environments, historical performance, and significant changes in the brand or reporting unit; if impairment is indicated, a quantitative assessment follows. In the quantitative assessment, fair value is determined using discounted cash flows, requiring estimates of future cash flows, sales growth rates, perpetuity growth, and a discount rate (weighted-average cost of capital) based on market data. Significant management judgment is required to estimate the impact of competitive, macroeconomic, and other factors—including those related to the COVID-19 pandemic—on future sales, operating profit, or cash flows. All assumptions used in impairment evaluations, such as forecasted growth rates and discount rates, are based on the best available market information and align with internal forecasts and operating plans; a deterioration in these assumptions could negatively affect results, and such risks are described in “Item 1A. Risk Factors.” Amortizable intangible assets are only evaluated for impairment if there is a significant change in operating or macroeconomic conditions; if undiscounted future cash flows indicate impairment, the asset is written down to its estimated fair value, which is based on discounted future cash flows. Reserves are established for tax positions that, despite being fully supportable, are likely to be challenged and ultimately not succeed; these reserves and related interest are adjusted based on audit progress, new tax laws, court cases, or settlements. An estimated annual effective tax rate is applied to quarterly operating results, and any significant or unusual item is separately calculated and recorded. Tax law requires items to be reported in tax returns at different times than in financial statements, resulting in differences between the annual tax rate in financial statements and the cash tax rate. Some differences are permanent (e.g., non-deductible expenses), and others reverse over time (e.g., depreciation), creating deferred tax assets and liabilities. Deferred tax assets represent future tax deductions or credits that have already been recognized in financial statements, and valuation allowances are established if it is not more likely than not that some portion or all of these assets will be realized. Deferred tax liabilities represent tax expenses deferred or expenses already deducted in tax returns but not yet recognized in financial statements. Interest ceases to accrue on notes or portions thereof called for redemption on or after the applicable redemption date, unless the issuer defaults in paying the redemption price and accrued interest. Additional interest will be paid to ensure that net payments to non-U.S. holders, after applicable U.S. or foreign tax withholdings, equal the amount due under the notes, subject to exceptions including taxes not imposed due to the holder’s trade or business in the U.S., permanent establishment, citizenship, being a personal holding company, passive foreign investment company, or controlled foreign corporation, being a 10-percent shareholder, being a bank receiving payments on a loan, taxes not imposed due to failure to comply with identification or reporting requirements, taxes imposed outside of withholding, taxes due to changes in law or interpretation more than 15 days after due date, estate, inheritance, gift, sales, excise, transfer, wealth, capital gains, or personal property taxes, withholding required by EU directives on savings, taxes required from a paying agent if another agent could make the payment without withholding, taxes due to late presentation of a note for payment more than 30 days after due date, and other specified taxes. The “Comparable Government Bond Rate” is the price (rounded to three decimal places, with 0.0005 rounded up) at which the gross redemption yield on the notes, if purchased on the third business day before redemption, would equal the gross redemption yield of the Comparable Government Bond on that day, based on the middle market price at 11:00 a.m. (London time). The “Comparable Government Bond” is a German government bond with maturity closest to the notes’ maturity, or another German government bond selected by an independent investment bank with advice from three German government bond brokers or market makers, as determined by such bank. “Remaining Scheduled Payments” refers to the remaining principal and interest payments due after the redemption date, except that if the redemption date is not an interest payment date, the next scheduled interest payment is reduced by the interest accrued to that date.

The indenture restricts the incurrence of debt secured by a lien on principal property or shares of stock of (or other interests in) any restricted subsidiary unless the company or that restricted subsidiary secures or causes it to secure such debt equally and ratably with (or prior to) such secured debt for as long as such debt is so secured. These restrictions do not apply to: (1) liens existing prior to the issuance of the notes; (2) liens on property or shares of stock of (or other interests in) or debt of any entity existing at the time it becomes a restricted subsidiary; (3) liens on property, shares, or debt of any entity (a) existing at the time of acquisition (including through merger or consolidation), (b) securing the purchase price of such property or shares or construction or improvement thereof, or (c) securing debt incurred prior to, at the time of, or within 365 days after the later of acquisition, completion of construction, or commencement of full operation of such property, or within 365 days after acquisition of such shares for financing purchase price or construction; (4) liens in favor of the company or any restricted subsidiary; (5) liens in favor of, or required by contracts with, governmental entities; or (6) extensions, renewals, or refundings of liens under any of the preceding clauses. Notwithstanding, the company or any restricted subsidiary may incur, suffer to exist, or guarantee such secured debt if, after giving effect thereto, the aggregate amount of such debt does not exceed 15% of the company’s consolidated net tangible assets. Consolidated net tangible assets are defined as the total amount of the company’s and its restricted subsidiaries’ assets minus all applicable depreciation, amortization, and other valuation reserves, all current liabilities (excluding intercompany liabilities), and all goodwill. The indenture does not restrict the transfer of principal property by the company to any unrestricted subsidiary or its ability to change the designation of a subsidiary owning principal property from a restricted to an unrestricted subsidiary; if such a change occurs, the unrestricted subsidiary would not be restricted from incurring secured debt, and the company would not be required to secure the notes equally and ratably with such debt upon such incurrence. The company may consolidate, merge with or into, or convey or transfer all or substantially all of its assets to any entity (including limited partnerships or limited liability companies), provided that: (i) the company remains the surviving corporation or, if not, the successor is a corporation organized and validly existing under the laws of any state of the United States or the District of Columbia and expressly assumes the company’s obligations under the indenture and the notes; (ii) immediately after the transaction, no event of default or default that would become an event of default with notice or lapse of time is in existence; and (iii) the company delivers to the trustee an opinion of counsel confirming compliance with the indenture. In the event of such a consolidation, merger, conveyance, transfer, or lease, the successor will succeed to and be substituted for the company as obligor on the notes with the same effect as if named in the indenture, and the company will be released from all obligations under the indenture and the notes.

The notes are issued under the laws of any state of the United States of America or the District of Columbia, and the issuer will expressly assume its obligations under the indenture and the notes through a supplemental indenture. Immediately after any consolidation, merger, conveyance, transfer, or lease, no event of default—nor any default or event that, after notice or lapse of time, would become an event of default—will be in existence or continuing, and the issuer will deliver to the trustee an opinion of counsel confirming that such transaction complies with the indenture. Any successor entity resulting from such transaction will succeed to and be substituted for the issuer as obligor on the notes with the same effect as if it had been named in the indenture, and the original issuer will be released from all obligations under the indenture and the notes. “Consolidated net tangible assets” are defined as the total assets of the issuer and its restricted subsidiaries minus all applicable depreciation, amortization, and valuation reserves; all current liabilities (excluding intercompany liabilities); and all goodwill, trade names, trademarks, patents, unamortized debt discount and expenses, and other like intangibles, as reported on the latest consolidated balance sheets prepared in accordance with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. “Debt” means any indebtedness for borrowed money. “Principal property” refers to any single manufacturing or processing plant, office building, or warehouse owned or leased by the issuer or any of its restricted subsidiaries, excluding any such property in the opinion of the Board of Directors that is not of material importance to the business. A “restricted subsidiary” is any subsidiary that is not an unrestricted subsidiary at the time. A “subsidiary” is any entity where at least a majority of the outstanding voting stock is owned, directly or indirectly, by the issuer or one or more of its subsidiaries. An “unrestricted subsidiary” is any subsidiary (not designated as restricted) that (1) primarily engages in finance, banking, credit, leasing, insurance, financial services, or similar operations, (2) has substantially all its assets consisting of the capital stock of one or more subsidiaries engaged in such operations, or (3) is designated as unrestricted by the Board of Directors. An “Event of Default” under the notes of a given series includes: (1) failure to pay interest when due, continuing for 30 days or more; (2) failure to pay principal or premium when due; (3) failure to pay any sinking or purchase fund obligation when due, continuing for 30 days or more; (4) breach of any covenant or warranty of PepsiCo (other than those in clauses 1–3) continuing for 90 days after written notice from the trustee or holders of at least 51% of the outstanding notes of the series; (5) certain bankruptcy, insolvency, reorganization, or administration events involving PepsiCo; or (6) any other event of default specified in the applicable prospectus supplement. If an Event of Default (other than clause 5) occurs and is continuing, the trustee or holders of at least 51% of the outstanding notes of the series may require immediate repayment of the entire principal amount of the notes (or a lesser amount as provided in the notes), together with all accrued and unpaid interest and premium. If an Event of Default under clause 5 occurs and is continuing, the entire principal amount of the outstanding notes (or a lesser amount as provided) will automatically become due and payable without any declaration or action by the trustee or holders. After a declaration of acceleration, holders of at least 51% of the outstanding notes of any series may rescind the accelerated payment if all existing Events of Default (except nonpayment of principal and interest resulting from the acceleration) have been cured or waived and if rescission would not conflict with any judgment or decree. Holders of a majority in principal amount of the outstanding notes of any series also have the right to waive past defaults, except defaults in paying principal, premium, or interest, or in respect of a covenant or provision that cannot be modified without the consent of all holders. Holders of at least 51% of the outstanding notes of a series may initiate a proceeding only after notifying the trustee in writing of a continuing Event of Default, making a written request with reasonable indemnity, and the trustee fails to act within 60 days, provided that the trustee has not received inconsistent directions from holders of a majority of the notes. These limitations do not apply to a suit by a holder for enforcement of payment of principal, interest, or premium after due dates. During an Event of Default, the trustee must exercise its rights and powers under the indenture with the care and skill of a prudent person, and is not required to act at the request or direction of holders unless such holders provide reasonable security or indemnity. Subject to certain provisions, holders of a majority in principal amount of the outstanding notes of any series may direct the time, method, and place of any proceeding for any remedy or exercise of trust or power conferred on the trustee. The trustee must give notice of any default to the holders of the notes of that series within 90 days after the default occurs, unless the default is already cured or waived, and may withhold notice if it determines in good faith that withholding is in the holders’ interest. The indenture may be amended or modified without holder consent to: (1) evidence a succession to the trustee; (2) cure ambiguities, defects, or inconsistencies; (3) provide for assumption of obligations in a merger, consolidation, or transfer of all or substantially all of the issuer’s assets; (4) provide additional rights or benefits to holders of a series; (5) add guarantors; (6) secure the notes of a series; (7) establish the form of notes of a series; (8) maintain the qualification of the indenture under the Trust Indenture Act; or (9) make any change that does not materially adversely affect any holder’s interests. Other amendments require consent of holders of not less than a majority of the aggregate principal amount of the outstanding notes of each affected series. However, no amendment may: (1) reduce the principal amount, interest, or premium payable or extend the fixed maturity; (2) alter or waive redemption provisions; (3) change the currency of payment; (4) reduce the percentage of notes required to consent to an amendment, supplement, or waiver; (5) impair the right to institute suit for enforcement of any payment; (6) waive a payment default with respect to the notes or any guarantor; (7) reduce the interest rate or extend the time for interest payment; (8) adversely affect the ranking of the notes; or (9) release any guarantor from its obligations under the guarantee or indenture, except in compliance with the terms of the indenture. The issuer may terminate its obligations under the indenture when: (1) all notes of any series authenticated and delivered have been delivered to the trustee for cancellation; or (2) all notes of any series not delivered for cancellation have become due and payable, will become due and payable within one year, or are to be redeemed within one year, and arrangements satisfactory to the trustee have been made for notice of redemption at the issuer’s expense, and in each case, sufficient funds have been irrevocably deposited with the trustee to pay and discharge all principal, interest, and premium, and all other sums due under the indenture, with delivery of an officers’ certificate and opinion of counsel stating all conditions precedent have been met. The issuer may elect to have its obligations discharged with respect to outstanding notes of any series (“legal defeasance”), meaning that the entire indebtedness will be deemed paid and discharged except for: (1) the rights of holders to receive principal, interest, and premium when due; (2) obligations regarding issuance of temporary notes, registration of transfer, mutilated, destroyed, lost, or stolen notes, and maintenance of an office or agency for security payments; (3) the rights, powers, trusts, duties, and immunities of the trustee; and (4) the defeasance provisions of the indenture. Additionally, the issuer may elect to release certain covenants in the indenture (“covenant defeasance”), meaning that omissions from compliance with those covenants will not constitute a default or event of default. In the event of covenant defeasance, certain events (excluding non-payment, bankruptcy, and insolvency) described under “Events of Default” will no longer constitute an event of default. To exercise either legal or covenant defeasance, the issuer must irrevocably deposit with the trustee as trust funds, specifically pledged and dedicated solely to the benefit of the holders of the series: (1) money in an amount; (2) U.S. government obligations (or equivalent government obligations for notes not denominated in U.S. dollars) that will provide, not later than one day before any payment due, money in an amount; or (3) a combination of money and U.S. government obligations (or equivalent), sufficient, as determined by a nationally recognized firm of independent registered public accountants, to pay and discharge all principal (including mandatory sinking fund payments), interest, and any premium at due date or maturity. For legal defeasance, the issuer must deliver to the trustee an opinion of counsel stating that, under then-applicable federal income tax law, holders of the notes of that series will not recognize income, gain, or loss for federal income tax purposes as a result of the defeasance and will be subject to the same federal income tax as if the defeasance had not occurred. For covenant defeasance, the issuer must deliver to the trustee an opinion of counsel to the same effect for U.S. federal income tax purposes. No event of default or default with respect to the outstanding notes of that series may be occurring or continuing at the time of such deposit, or in the case of legal defeasance, no bankruptcy or insolvency default may occur or be continuing on or before the 91st day after the deposit, with the condition not being deemed satisfied until after the 91st day. The defeasance must not create a conflicting interest for the trustee under the Trust Indenture Act, assuming all notes of the series were in default under such Act. The defeasance must not breach or violate any other agreement or instrument to which the issuer is a party. The trust arising from such deposit must not constitute an investment company under the Investment Company Act of 1940, as amended, unless registered or exempt from registration. The issuer must deliver to the trustee an officers’ certificate and opinion of counsel stating all conditions precedent with respect to the defeasance have been met. The PepsiCo International Retirement Plan Defined Contribution Program (PIRP-DC) was amended and restated effective January 1, 2021, with updates through December 2021. The Plan was originally established by PepsiCo, Inc. on September 1, 1980, and was amended and restated on September 2, 1982. It was further amended on October 1, 2003, when the Plan Rules became the “Plan A Rules” (for benefits funded by Corporation contributions) and “Plan B Rules” (for benefits funded as they arise). On January 1, 2005, it was modified so that no person subject to U.S. taxation may have their right to a benefit increased or created, instead being treated as if they had permanently left the Corporation and its Associated Companies before becoming subject to U.S. taxation. On January 1, 2010, the Plan A and Plan B Rules were fully amended and restated into a single document, which includes the terms of the “DB Program,” and the prior amendment remains in effect. On January 1, 2011, a new defined contribution structure (the “DC Program”) was established for selected international employees, including those on assignments outside their home countries where participation in home country plans is impractical and senior globalists on U.S. tax equalized packages. The DC Program’s terms are set forth in this document, which serves as the governing legal document for the DC Program. The DC Program was previously amended and restated on January 1, 2016, to include selected employees who were localized to a country outside their home country, were previously participating in a defined benefit or defined contribution plan, and have no company-provided retirement program available. On January 1, 2019, the DC Program was amended to recognize same-sex and opposite-sex domestic partners for certain purposes for Members actively employed or on authorized leave of absence on or after January 1, 2019. The DC Program was again amended and restated effective January 1, 2021. The Plan is unfunded and unsecured under U.S. Internal Revenue Code and ERISA, and benefits of executives are obligations of their individual employers, with executives having the rights of unsecured general creditors. The Plan is also intended to be exempt from ERISA as a plan maintained outside the United States primarily for the benefit of nonresident aliens. In Article II, definitions include: “Approved Transfer” as a transfer to or secondment in the U.S. or a change in employment circumstances making a Member a U.S. Person, approved by the Corporation or a Member’s Employer; “Associated Company” as any company controlled or associated with PepsiCo, which agrees to perform and observe the DC Program terms; “Corporation” as PepsiCo, Inc., or its successor; “Dependant” as the person receiving the balance of a Member’s PIRP-DC Account upon death; “DB Program” as the defined benefit portion of the Plan; “DC Program” as the defined contribution portion; “Distribution Valuation Date” as the date set by the Vice President for valuation of accounts, currently the month end after a distribution trigger, with adjustments for non-business days, and may be changed by the Vice President; “Effective Date” as January 1, 2011; “Eligible Domestic Partner” as an individual of the same or opposite sex who meets criteria under civil union, Cigna enrollment, or written specification by the Vice President, with claims required within 60 days of death, and the term does not apply to an Eligible Spouse; “Eligible Employee” as someone employed exclusively outside the U.S. on a full-time salaried basis, not accruing DB benefits, and meeting one of four criteria: assignment outside home country with impractical participation in home country plans; second or more consecutive assignments outside home country with no Corporation or affiliated company plan available; senior globalists on U.S. tax equalized packages; or localization with prior participation in a retirement program and no local plan; the Vice President may designate part-time employees as Eligible Employees if they otherwise meet the criteria; “Eligible Spouse” as the individual to whom the Member is married or was married at death, determined by the law of the Member’s principal residence, with only one Eligible Spouse allowed; “Employers” as PepsiCo and its Associated Companies, with “Approved Employer” meaning one approved by the Vice President to allow Eligible Employees to become and remain Active Members; “Entry Date” as the date specified by the Vice President for admission to Membership; “Interest Credit” as the annual credit to a Member’s PIRP-DC Account under Section 4.01(b); and “Interest Rate” as the annualized rate used to determine the Interest Credit, effective as of January 1, 2011.

For purposes of the DC Program, a Member shall have only one Eligible Spouse. “Employers” refers to the Corporation and any Associated Company, with the specific Employer determined by context or circumstances; “Employer” in relation to a person means the Employer in whose employment that person was or is at the relevant time, or, if more than one, those Employers during the relevant period. The Vice President may change the basis for determining the Interest Rate from time to time to ensure it is readily determinable and administrable and reasonably expected to provide a substantially market rate, but the Interest Rate shall not exceed a level considered earnings under Treasury Regulation § 1.409A-1(o). “Member” means an Eligible Employee admitted to Membership under Article III and who remains entitled to a benefit under the DC Program; in relation to each Employer, a Member means one in or formerly in its employment. “Active Member” and “Inactive Member” have the respective meanings defined in Section 3.03. “Pay Credit” is the credit made to an Active Member’s PIRP-DC Account under Section 4.01(a). “Plan” refers to the PepsiCo International Retirement Plan, which includes the DC Program and DB Program. “Plan Year” is a 12-consecutive-month period beginning January 1 and ending December 31 of the same calendar year. “PepsiCo Organization” means the controlled group of organizations of which the Corporation is a part, as defined by U.S. Internal Revenue Code section 414 and related regulations; an entity is only considered part of the PepsiCo Organization during the period it is part of that group. “PIRP-DC Account” is an unfunded, notional account maintained for a Member on the books of the Member’s Employer to indicate the dollar amount credited under the DC Program; the balance is determined according to interpretive principles and decisions applied by the Vice President. “Salary” means (i) home notional base salary for an Eligible Employee not paid on a U.S. payroll, and (ii) base salary plus annual bonus for one paid on a U.S. payroll; notwithstanding this, for Eligible Employees not paid on a U.S. payroll who become Active Members on or after January 1, 2021, Salary includes home notional base salary plus annual bonus. The Vice President determines Salary and such determination is conclusive and binding. “Service” is the period of continuous employment (including all permissible periods of authorized leave of absence) with any Approved Employer; a permissible period of authorized leave of absence is not more than 12 months, unless individually authorized in writing by the Vice President. A break in service of less than 12 months does not break continuity of Service; other breaks (including those of 12 months or more or before becoming a Member) break continuity, and prior employment may be counted only if it would otherwise qualify and is approved by the Vice President. For a transfer from non-Eligible to Eligible Employee status with an Approved Employer, pre-transfer employment may be counted only with Vice President approval; similarly, post-transfer employment with another Employer may be counted only with approval. Service does not include periods of employment prior to an entity becoming an Employer or a member of the PepsiCo Organization. “Status Change” means any change in a Member’s circumstances (other than an Approved Transfer) that causes the Member to become a U.S. Person. “U.S. Person” means (1) a U.S. citizen; (2) a person lawfully admitted for permanent residence in the U.S. at any time during the calendar year or who has applied for such residence; or (3) a resident alien under U.S. Internal Revenue Code section 7701(b)(1)(A), including those meeting the substantial presence test or making an election to be treated as a U.S. resident. Additionally, a person is considered a U.S. Person for Section 9.14 purposes in any year requiring filing of a U.S. individual income tax return, unless the Vice President determines it is clear the person has no U.S. source earned income from a PepsiCo Organization member. “Valuation date” is each business day as determined by the Vice President, as of which Members’ PIRP-DC Accounts are valued (except for distributions under Article VI); as of the Effective Date, the DC Program has a Valuation Date for all Members on the last day of each Plan Year. The Vice President may change any current Valuation Date, with adjustments applied to prevent duplicate or disproportionate benefits as determined by the Vice President. Gender and number references are inclusive unless context indicates otherwise; a period of 365 consecutive days (or 366 if including February 29) constitutes a year, and for benefit calculations involving partial years or months, a proportionate amount may be given.
